newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Amnesty says Nigeria contemptuous of human rights.
newsitem.headline: Amnesty says Nigeria contemptuous of human rights.

text.p: Human rights group Amnesty International accused Nigeria's military government on Wednesday of being openly contemptuous of human rights.

In a report on Africa's most populous country, Amnesty said little had changed for the better in Nigeria since it drew worldwide outrage last year when it hanged author Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight minority rights activists of the Ogoni tribe.

"As the first anniversary of their execution draws near, little has changed," said the London-based group, adding: "The present military government in Nigeria has a record of open contempt for human rights."
"The government continues to violate the human rights of its critics, including opposition politicians, journalists, human rights activists and members of the Ogoni ethnic group."

The report was released ahead of the November 10 anniversary of the executions of the men who were found guilty of the murder of four Ogoni chiefs by a tribunal seen by critics of the Nigerian government as an unfair trial.
Nigeria's special duties minister Wada Nas on Monday accused Amnesty International of planning to cause trouble in the country by organising demonstrations to mark the anniversary.
Police at the same time said they were aware of plans to disturb public peace in the volatile and oil-rich Ogoniland and vowed to "deal ruthlessly" with any demonstrators.

Amnesty International officials said they would launch a campaign against Nigeria to push for democratic reforms and had drafted a 10-point demand for Nigerian authorities, which included a call for the release of political detainees.
Other demands were for a guarantee of fair trials for accused persons and the abolition of the death penalty.
"Surely the time has come to break with the past by ending the contempt for human rights in Nigeria," the Amnesty International report said.
"Without the urgent establishment of respect for human rights in Nigeria, the transition to civilian rule should be viewed with deep scepticism by the international community."
Military ruler General Sani Abacha is implementing a transition programme of phased elections which he says would usher in an elected civilian government by October 1998.
Nigeria has been ruled by the military for most of the time since independence from Britain in 1960.
Nigeria plunged into turmoil in 1993 when a presidential vote presumed to have been won by millionaire businessman Moshood Abiola was annulled by the army.
Abiola has been detained since 1994 when he proclaimed himself president in defiance of Abacha, who seized power in the mayhem that followed the annulment.
Several opposition men are also in detention or have fled abroad since strikes and riots were organised in 1994 to force Abacha to cede power to Abiola.
The government maintains there are no political prisoners in Nigeria and that those detained are held for specific offences.

About half a dozen detainees have been released since the United Nations sent a fact-finding mission to Nigeria. The U.N. report endorsed Abacha's transition to civil rule programme but called for detainees to be freed and draconian laws reformed.
